subject: Opalyn committed capacity: throughput, SLO headroom, and next steps
messages:
From: Samir Gupta <samir@opalyn.ai>
To: Markus Klein <markus_klein@redwood.ai>
Cc: Opalyn Procurement <procurement@opalyn.ai>
Date: Sun, 12 Dec 2027 09:14:00 -0800
Subject: Dedicated commit sizing — current traffic profile and ask

Hi Markus,

Thanks again for the demo last week. Procurement asked me to scope the committed capacity we talked about. I pulled together a short token profile (attached) with our expected steady and peak behavior. Short version:
- Baseline steady: ~2,200 tokens/sec (avg) across our US region during business hours
- Daily peak spikes: up to 7,500 tokens/sec for sustained 10–20 minute windows (product events)
- Long-tail requests (LTV background jobs) add ~500 tokens/sec mostly off-peak
- Model: opalyn-chat-13B (we plan to move to a 13B optimized variant). P95 latency target for interactive flows is 350 ms.

Two asks: 1) can Redwood map that to a Dedicated slab sizing (GPU count / SKU) and expected p95 latency/observed tokens/sec per slab? 2) what safety/headroom would you recommend for a commit that balances cost but avoids SLA risk?

I attached opalyn_token_profile.csv with the hourly breakdown. Procurement is watching renewal cadence, so if we can turn this into a simple commit proposal + expected SLA fit, that helps move this forward.

Cheers,
Samir
Samir Gupta
Head of Platform
Opalyn

Attachment: opalyn_token_profile.csv (CSV, 12KB)
From: Markus Klein <markus_klein@redwood.ai>
To: Samir Gupta <samir@opalyn.ai>
Cc: Opalyn Procurement <procurement@opalyn.ai>
Date: Sun, 12 Dec 2027 13:02:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Dedicated commit sizing — current traffic profile and ask

Samir — thanks for the profile, this is very clear. A quick read-through and a couple of high level recommendations:

1) Slab sizing (initial suggestion)
   - For opalyn-chat-13B (quantized 8-bit hybrid path) we estimate ~750 tokens/sec per A100-80GB equivalent GPU under typical 1–2k seq streaming patterns.
   - To cover your stated peak of 7,500 tokens/sec we’d map that to ~10 GPUs (750 * 10 = 7,500) for steady peak coverage.

2) Safety / headroom
   - We recommend a 25–30% operational headroom above customer peak for committed slabs to account for KV cache churn, model switchovers, and regional re-routes. That pushes to 13 GPUs (~7,500 * 1.30 / 750 ≈ 13).
   - If you want a firm p95 < 350 ms target, add an additional 10% buffer for tail-latency sensitive flows (can be done via a small burst pool).

3) Latency notes
   - The 750 tok/s/GPU baseline assumes continuous batching and 1–2 active request segments; for long contexts (8k tokens) throughput per GPU drops ~20% — we’ll call that out in the model.

4) Proposed next step
   - I’ll circulate a short SLO/headroom workbook and a pricing draft; can you confirm whether quiet-hours/off-peak jobs can be throttled or scheduled? That helps significantly with price tiers.

Putting Ben and Karthik on the thread to finalize the headroom math and pull in a short excel with scenario runs.

— Markus
Markus Klein

Redwood Inference

Markus / team — did a quick sensitivity pass and attached the scenario exports in slo_headroom_model.xlsx. Highlights below:

- Baseline assumptions (from Samir’s CSV): avg seq length ~280 tokens, peak window avg 10–20 minutes as noted.
- Throughput per GPU (measured): 750 tok/s (1–2k seq streaming), 600 tok/s for sustained 8k contexts.
- Recommended committed slab for cost/latency balance: 14 GPUs (gives ~10.5k tok/s nominal at 750 tok/s/GPU). This supports your 7.5k peak with ~40% headroom which buys down tail risk and avoids relying on burst lanes.
- Burst policy: 2-GPU burst pool attached to dedicated slab for 90th-percentile events. That plus 14 GPUs keeps p95 below 350ms in our lab with KV cache warmed.

Tradeoffs: 14 GPUs increases commit cost by ~12–18% vs the minimal 13-GPU headroom plan, but reduces probability of SLA exceedance by ~4x in our Monte Carlo traffic model.

Notes for procurement: we flagged a mid-term checkpoint at month 3 to evaluate observed peak vs modeled. If Opalyn can sched long-running LTV jobs to off-peak windows, effective needed committed GPUs can drop by 2–3.

Attachment: slo_headroom_model.xlsx (Excel, 92KB)

-Karthik

Adding a couple operational details that will be in the pricing + runbook:

- Cold-starts and KV cache: for chat flows we assume a 15–20% token-rate hit on initial user sessions until cache warms. We model that as applied to the first 5 minutes of a surge.
- Quantization: the 13B optimized variant has two runtime modes — FP16 (higher memory, slightly higher throughput) and 8-bit hybrid (lower mem, ~5–10% lower throughput but cost saving). We included both in the workbook.
- Canary & rollback: propose a 2-week canary during month 1; if p95 breaches > 1.5x target more than 3 times we trigger a capacity/traffic shift.

I’m attaching the draft pricing (dedicated_pricing_draft.pdf) that lines up with Karthik’s 14-GPU recommendation and includes a burst-lane add-on. Markus — please confirm whether Opalyn wants the 8-bit default or we price both options.

Laura Bennett
Solutions Engineering
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Dedicated commit sizing — current traffic profile and ask

Samir — thanks, looping everything together here with a short recommendation pack so procurement has a decision path. TL;DR: recommend a 12+2 (committed 12 GPUs + 2-GPU burst lane) or a conservative committed 14 GPUs (no burst lane).

Why the two options:
- 12+2 (cost-efficient): covers the 7.5k observed peak with ~30% operational headroom when burst lanes are available. Lower monthly commit cost; reliant on burst lane for very tight tail events.
- 14 committed (robust): ~40% headroom, removes reliance on burst pools, better for guaranteed p95 < 350 ms without special routing. Slightly higher commit cost, recommended if Opalyn expects frequent product-event spikes.

Requested next steps:
1) Confirm which option Procurement prefers (12+2 or 14 committed).
2) Confirm runtime default: 8-bit hybrid or FP16 for the canary period. 8-bit saves ~12% on unit cost but we should note the throughput delta.
3) We’ll put a 3-month review checkpoint into the contract and include the runbook for throttling long-running jobs.

I attached the SLO & headroom workbook and the pricing draft for procurement to review. If you want, we can lock the canary start date in next week and provision a temporary test slab for two days so Opalyn can run a production-like spike test.

Thanks — happy to jump on a quick call if procurement wants to walk the tradeoffs.

— Markus
